AI Supply Chain: TSMC to expand 3nm capacity for major AI customer's growth?
Additional 3nm wafer supply would fuel more growth of AI semis in 2026. We also see potential upside to our existing TSMC capex of US\$43bn in 2026.
Major AI customer asks TSMC to build more wafer capacity. In our previous AI Supply Chain tracker, we mentioned that CoWoS was not really the major constraint factor; rather it was TSMC’s wafer front-end and ABF substrate supply in 1H26 (give the T-Glass shortage). Alchip also reaffirmed a 3nm wafer shortage (link). We held the view that TSMC 2026 capex could only be US\$43bn (up from US\$41bn in 2025), as TSMC wanted to keep its leading-edge capacity full, not just for 2026, but also future years. However, after Nvidia (covered by Joseph Moore) CEO’s Taiwan visit last weekend, the plan for its 3nm capacity may have changed (see Nvidia CEO Huang sees strong demand for Blackwell chips).
1. Our channel checks suggest an additional 20k of 3nm capacity could be added in Taiwan fab: According to TSMC’s management on its earnings call, all new clean room space in Taiwan would be for 2nm expansion, while 3nm expansion would need to happen in existing fabs. Now, since TSMC has decided to add 20kwpm more 3nm in Taiwan, clean room space is becoming the key issue. Our latest checks suggest TSMC may move 22nm/28nm out of Fab15 (and reserve those tools for a future Europe fab). By adding 20k more 3nm capacity, or US\$5-7bn capex (assuming US\$300mn per k), would imply its 2026 capex reaching US\$48-50bn, similar to bull camp assumptions – a potential positive catalyst to semicap.
2. Follow up research on our power capacity vs. CoWoS capacity. Our analysis on what 10GW of Nvidia’s Rubin chips would mean to TSMC’s CoWoS capacity has gained traction. By increasing the project pipeline (other mega and hyper power deployment plans), we still conclude that TSMC’s CoWoS capacity should be sufficient (see Exhibit 3 ). Please also see Exhibit 18 for our cloud capex and AI server capex update.
3. ASIC design service update: TSMC and its subsidiary GUC are working together to service Tesla (covered by Adam Jonas), and enable its 3nm AI5 design and production. Of note, AI5 will continue to use LPDDR instead of HBM, and hence we are not changing our TSMC CoWoS capacity assumptions. We raised our GUC PT to US\$2,288 (link). And in our TSMC: Thoughts about auto semi foundry dynamics, we mentioned a US\$2bn foundry opportunity a year for the 2nm Tesla AI6 chip.
Stock implications: We stay OW on TSMC (Top Pick)/KYEC/ASE on potential better AI semi growth. The potential 3nm capex hike could be positive to global semicap sentiment. We are also OW on selective ASIC names, such as GUC/Alchip.

2026 AI supply upside may hinge on TSMC 3nm capacity Our assumption for TSMC 3nm capacity is that it should be around 110-120kwpm for 2025 and then grow to 140-150kwpm by 2026. The incremental capacity includes 20kwpm from TSMC's AZ fab phase 2 and another 10kwpm conversion from 4/5nm in Taiwan. However, we have been hearing that several TSMC customers may have had difficulty securing enough 3nm capacity at TSMC, including Nvidia, AMD and Alchip (see Nvidia CEO Huang sees strong demand for Blackwell chips). As a result, our recent checks suggest that TSMC is now considering to expand 3nm capacity 20kwpm further than our initial expectation. However, clean room space is the problem for expansion, as TSMC currently cannot find clean room for it (all the new clean room space will be for 2nm, according to TSMC’s management on the earnings call). Our latest checks suggest that TSMC may move its 22nm/28nm out from Fab15, and move to a European fab. If this took place, it would imply 2026 capex rising to US\$48-50bn, assuming US\$300mn capex per k wafer of 3nm.

Calculating the power deployment demand for CoWoS We published our power deployment implied CoWoS analysis in the last issue of our AI tracker (see note). Many investors were curious about what the currently announced power deployment plans implied for CoWoS demand. We thus gathered the mega and hyper power deployment plans that we see right now, and if the usage of chips is not specified, we use NVIDIA GPU and ASICs as a reference. We calculated the racks needed for each project based on power consumption, and summed up the chips volume housed in these racks. Thus, the implied CoWoS number is 1.24mn for total consumption, which implies 681k units of CoWoS demand annually vs. TSMC and non-TSMC CoWoS average annual capacity of nearly 1,100k. We think this is in-line with our understanding that CoWoS is not the key bottleneck, while front-end capacity and other materials, such as Tglass, are the potential products in shortage.

We also try to calculate the demand for both TSMC and non-TSMC CoWoS based on the currently announced partnerships, including the OpenAI-NVIDIA 10GW, OpenAI-AMD 6GW, and Google-Anthropic 1GW contracts. Our analysis shows that total implied CoWoS consumption for TSMC stands at 629k wafers and 110k for the non-TSMC camp. By assuming that both the OpenAI-NVIDIA and OpenAI-AMD contracts will be realized in three years, we expect 2027 annual CoWoS demand from these projects would be 245k for TSMC and 37k for the non-TSMC camp. The implied 3nm wafer consumption could be 260k for Nvidia (OpenAI), 70k for Broadcom (Anthropic), and 2nm wafer consumption of 81k for AMD (OpenAI) project, based on the announced partnerships. 3 Morgan Stanley丨 RESEARCH Idea Morgan Stanley Research

Global AI capex: remains strong after Oracle's print
Exhibit 17: TSMC is expected to produce 5.1mn chips in 2025, which could be fully digested in 1H26 based on Oracle's announced strong AI server build in 2026
Hyperscalers' capex remains strong into 2026
According to our US hardware analyst Erik Woodring's Global Cloud Capex Tracker, Morgan Stanley expects 2026 cloud capex to increase to US\$621bn, implying 33% Y/Y growth (vs. consensus now at only +25% Y/Y).
Assuming the proportion of AI server capex (spending on short-lived assets) increases, implied AI server capex may grow \~73% Y/Y in 2026 (see Exhibit 18 ). This underscores our Attractive industry view on Greater China Semis – we see AI demand remaining strong. In AI semis, and we are OW on TSMC, Samsung Electronics, Alchip, Aspeed, and KYEC.

Monthly tokens processed by major CSPs suggest that AI inference demand is growing
We see growing AI inference demand, as evidenced by the rapidly growing number of tokens processed by major CSPs. China's token consumption reached 30trn daily as of end-June 2025 (monthly run-rate was 900trn), +300x vs. 0.1trn daily at the beginning of 2024 (as reported by the National Data Administration of China). Google (covered by Brian Nowak) processed over 1,300trn tokens in September 2025, +33% from 980trn in July 2025. Bytedance's token consumption reached 30trn daily as of end-September 2025 (monthly run-rate was 900trn), +83% vs. 16.4trn daily as of end-May 2025. Microsoft (covered by Keith Weiss) processed over 500trn tokens through its Foundry APIs in F2025 (year end June 2025), up over 7x Y/Y.
